topics.title: Postgres LISTEN/NOTIFY doesn't 'not scale' — you're just holding it wrong
topics.summary: DBOS benchmarked naive LISTEN/NOTIFY usage against a batched-flush approach and found a 20x throughput jump (2.9K to 60K writes/sec) by working around the global exclusive lock Postgres takes on commit when NOTIFY is involved, which blocks group commit. Worth a deep dive into why that lock exists, when LISTEN/NOTIFY is still the wrong tool (once it's the source of truth rather than a ping), and how to build the buffer-and-batch-with-polling-fallback pattern in a real service.

topics.title: How a security camera shipped a GitHub org admin token to every customer's browser
topics.summary: A researcher found a live GitHub admin token (with access to hundreds of Hanwha repos) embedded in a consumer security camera's web UI, reachable in ~30 files after decrypting the firmware. Root cause: a Vite CI build step that dumped the entire build environment into client-shipped files. A concrete case study on why 'don't leak secrets into frontend bundles' needs to be enforced by tooling (CI secret scanning, minimal-scope build tokens, bundle auditing) rather than developer discipline, especially on embedded/IoT build pipelines that get less scrutiny than web apps.

topics.title: Why Netflix built its own LLM serving stack instead of just calling a managed API
topics.summary: Netflix's platform team moved LLM inference into their existing production environment rather than standing up a separate ML silo, making explicit calls on engine selection, model packaging, API surface design, and output-constraint enforcement. A good angle piece on the build-vs-buy tradeoff for LLM infra at a company that already has serious platform muscle — when does in-house serving actually pay off versus when it's resume-driven infra work, and what does 'production revealed X' actually mean in practice.

topics.title: When your infrastructure provider force-upgrades your database out from under you
topics.summary: ThriveCart's July 3, 2026 outage started when their infra provider triggered a forced, unscheduled upgrade on a core production database, knocking it offline for ~10 hours. Unlike most postmortems about self-inflicted config errors, this is the 'the outage wasn't your bug, it was your dependency's maintenance policy' case — a chance to write about designing for provider-initiated failovers you don't control: read replicas you can promote unilaterally, contractual notice windows, and testing failover paths you never chose to trigger yourself.

topics.title: Coinbase's 50-minute outage started with a 'routine' config update — what blast-radius controls were missing
topics.summary: Coinbase's July 14, 2026 incident took down transfers, card transactions, and onchain services for ~50 minutes after a routine configuration update misconfigured a core network component. Pair this with other 2026 'routine change' outages into a piece on why 'routine' is the most dangerous word in an infra changelog: staged rollouts, automated config diffing/validation, and blast-radius limiting for network-layer changes specifically (as opposed to app-layer deploys, which usually get more guardrails).
